meta.title: Who really said "All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Shakespeare: spoken by Jaques in As You Like It, act 2 scene 7, first printed in the 1623 First Folio. The metaphor itself was already old.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players'?
meta.ogDescription: Real and sourced: Jaques in As You Like It, act 2 scene 7, printed in the 1623 First Folio. But Shakespeare did not invent the metaphor.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Spoken by the melancholy Jaques in As You Like It, Act 2, Scene 7 — the opening of the “seven ages of man” speech. The wording is confirmed in the play’s edited text at the Folger Shakespeare Library ↗, and the play was first published in the 1623 First Folio ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: As You Like It, Act 2, Scene 7
Jaques, answering Duke Senior in the Forest of Arden

source.excerpt:
DUKE SENIOR
Thou seest we are not all alone unhappy.
This wide and universal theater
Presents more woeful pageants than the scene
Wherein we play in.

JAQUES
All the world’s a stage,
And all the men and women merely players.
They have their exits and their entrances,
And one man in his time plays many parts,
His acts being seven ages.
trail: Believed 1599: Shakespeare writes As You Like It, working from Thomas Lodge’s prose romance Rosalynde (first published 1590). Wikipedia on the play’s date and source ↗
4 August 1600: the play is entered in the Stationers’ Register as a work “to be stayed” — publication blocked, for reasons never established. Details of the entry ↗
1623: the speech reaches print for the first time in the First Folio. The Folger notes that this text “serves as the source for all subsequent editions of the play.” Folger Shakespeare Library ↗
Today: Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ places the speech at Act II, scene vii, spoken by Jaques, with the same wording the Folio-derived editions give.
source.excerptNote: Modern-spelling text from the Folger Shakespeare edition of Act 2, Scene 7 ↗. In the 1623 Folio the second line is spelled with “meerely Players” — see the Internet Shakespeare Editions F1 transcription ↗.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: Who was William Shakespeare?
author.bio: Shakespeare wrote As You Like It around 1599, near the peak of his working life, adapting Thomas Lodge’s prose romance Rosalynde (1590) into a comedy set in the Forest of Arden. The play was never printed in his lifetime: it was entered in the Stationers’ Register in 1600 marked “to be stayed”, and only reached print in the 1623 First Folio, seven years after his death. That Folio text is the source of every later edition — including the one this line is quoted from.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The words really are Shakespeare’s, and they are pinned to a scene. What gets misattributed is everything around them — the idea, the exact wording, the speaker’s standing, and the tidy origin story.

items.why: Life-as-theatre was stock imagery long before 1599. Erasmus asks in The Praise of Folly (1511) what life is “but a kind of play in which men in various costumes perform”; Richard Edwards’ Damon and Pythias, written the year Shakespeare was born, has “Pythagoras said that this world was like a stage / Whereon many play their parts”; and the Latin phrase behind them, attributed to Petronius, was circulating in England at the time. Wikipedia collects the antecedents ↗

items.who: “and all the men and women are merely players”
items.why: The Folio-derived text has no “are”. Both the Folger edition ↗ and Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ read “And all the men and women merely players.” The padded variant is common enough that Wikipedia’s own article ↗ quotes the line with “are” in it.

The line belongs to the play’s professional cynic, and he does not even start the metaphor: in the lines immediately before, Duke Senior has just called the world a “wide and universal theater”. Jaques is capping someone else’s consolation, not delivering an authorial creed. See the exchange in context ↗

items.who: The Globe’s motto, Totus mundus agit histrionem
items.why: It is often repeated that Shakespeare was simply Englishing his own playhouse’s motto. Wikipedia says only that the Globe “may have used” it ↗, and Tiffany Stern devoted a whole article to the question — ‘Was Totus Mundus Agit Histrionem ever the Motto of the Globe Theatre?’, Theatre Notebook 51 (1997) ↗. Treat it as a nice story, not a documented fact.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine and locatable: Jaques, As You Like It, Act 2, Scene 7, first printed in the 1623 First Folio ↗. The sentence is Shakespeare’s; the metaphor was borrowed goods.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The speech works because it is a consolation that curdles. Duke Senior, exiled and cold, reaches for a comforting thought — other people suffer too, the world is a “wide and universal theater” full of sadder scenes than ours. Jaques, the play’s designated cynic, takes the metaphor off him and runs it to the end of a human life, cataloguing seven ages that begin with a mewling infant.

So the most quoted sentence in the play is not a thesis Shakespeare is advancing. It is a character seizing someone else’s figure of speech and pushing it somewhere bleaker than intended — which is exactly why it survives being lifted out of the scene and printed on a mug.
context.detailsSummary: The theatrum mundi tradition Shakespeare was working in
detailsBody: Life-as-theatre was a Renaissance commonplace before Jaques opened his mouth. Erasmus asks in The Praise of Folly (1511) what human life is “but a kind of play in which men in various costumes perform until the director motions them off the stage.” Richard Edwards’ play Damon and Pythias, written the year Shakespeare was born, has: “Pythagoras said that this world was like a stage / Whereon many play their parts.” Behind both sits a Latin tag attributed to Petronius, quod fere totus mundus exercet histrionem, which circulated widely in Shakespeare’s England ↗.

That the idea was second-hand is the point rather than a debunking. Shakespeare’s contribution is compression: eleven syllables that do what a paragraph of Erasmus does, in a line short enough to remember.
context.pull: Shakespeare didn’t invent the metaphor. He wrote the version nobody could improve on.
